history: The Autódromo Internacional Nelson Piquet, commonly known as Jacarepaguá, was a motorsport complex built in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Opened in 1978, it was named after Formula One champion Nelson Piquet. The circuit hosted the Brazilian Grand Prix on several occasions, initially in the early 1980s and later in the late 1980s after a switch from Interlagos. Besides Formula One, Jacarepaguá also hosted major motorcycle events and Brazilian national racing series. The 'Short' layout, a shortened configuration of the main track, was often used for national-level racing and club events, providing a more accessible and economical option for smaller series and driver training. The complex was eventually demolished in 2012 to make way for facilities for the 2016 Summer Olympics, marking the end of an era for Brazilian motorsport.
atmosphere: Imagine standing trackside at Jacarepaguá during a Stock Car Brasil race on the Short layout. The air is thick with the smell of high-octane fuel and burning rubber. The roar of the V8 engines reverberates through your chest as the cars power out of the Descida do Lago, jostling for position heading into the Arquibancada corner. The Brazilian fans, passionate and vibrant, cheer wildly from the grandstands, waving flags and chanting. There's a raw, visceral energy to the racing here, a sense of untamed speed and fearless competition.
trackCharacter: The Short layout at Jacarepaguá is a fast, flowing circuit that emphasizes power and handling balance. Its relatively simple design allows drivers to maintain high average speeds, making it a thrilling challenge for those who dare to push the limits. Unlike the longer Grand Prix layouts, the Short configuration eliminates some of the more technical corners, creating a more streamlined and aggressive driving experience. The emphasis is on momentum and maximizing corner exit speed to carry as much pace as possible onto the next straight.

historySnippets: The original circuit was very bumpy, leading to complaints from drivers.
Alain Prost won the first F1 race at Jacarepaguá in 1982.
The Short layout was frequently used for national Stock Car races.
The circuit was demolished to make way for the 2016 Rio Olympics.
Ayrton Senna achieved multiple podiums at Jacarepaguá but never won.
weatherNotes: Rio de Janeiro has a tropical climate, meaning that high temperatures and humidity are common year-round. Rain showers, often heavy and sudden, can significantly impact grip levels, particularly on the slick asphalt of the Short layout. Tire management is crucial in both wet and dry conditions due to the abrasive surface.
drivingAdvice: On the Short layout, maintaining momentum is key. Focus on smooth inputs and minimizing wheelspin, particularly on corner exits. Aggressively attack the Descida do Lago to set up overtakes into Curva Sul. Be mindful of tire wear, especially during longer races, and conserve energy by managing your pace strategically. The Retão offers the prime overtaking opportunity; position your car carefully to maximize your slipstream and braking advantage.
famousRaces: Stock Car Brasil races on the Short layout were known for their intense battles and close finishes.
Brazilian national racing series events held on the Short layout provided a platform for up-and-coming drivers to showcase their talent.
Club racing events on the Short layout were popular among amateur racers and motorsport enthusiasts.
localCulture: Rio de Janeiro is famous for its vibrant culture, stunning beaches, and iconic landmarks. The local cuisine features delicious seafood, feijoada (a black bean stew), and refreshing caipirinhas. Paddock life at Jacarepaguá was always lively, with samba music often playing and fans enthusiastically supporting their favorite drivers. The passion for motorsport runs deep in Brazil, and the atmosphere at the track reflected the country's love for racing.
